clue:fresno.text: Julian’s song. He only plays it once a month. “You said the wall was where you yelled at God / I never heard Him yell back.” Lena left in the second chorus. So did I. Thursday the 8th, Margot was there. Lena by the window, alone. She left in the second chorus again.
clue:fresno.title: “Fresno”

clue:nora_box.text: A banker’s box in the RA storage closet since April: CALLOWAY · 222 · HOLD FOR FAMILY. HOLD underlined twice. A Selma High sweatshirt, CDs, a mug, a picture of two girls laughing in a dorm window — one of them Priya. A composition book. Inside the cover: Nora Calloway · Delgado 222 · If found, please return. Reward: I’ll sing you something. Priya has never gotten past that page. Nobody came for it. It lives in 401 now.
clue:nora_box.title: Hold for family

clue:plaque.text: Small brass plate under the candles: NORA GRACE CALLOWAY, 1989–2009. “Lord, to whom shall we go?” Somebody’s daughter.
clue:plaque.title: A plaque at the shrine

clue:postcard.text: She read the back of my postcard twice. Asked who A.H. was like she didn’t care. She cared. Hale’s table: he buys them at Blackwell’s by the hundred and has used three. Mine was nine pages. Lena wrote him twelve. She has one too.
clue:postcard.title: The postcard

note:alarm.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log. Tuesday the 6th, nothing. Either the theory’s wrong or he’s on vacation. Alarm 3, Tuesday the 13th, 3:20, in a storm, under the overhang: twenty-five days. Margot says he’s irregular or he’s two people. Alarm 4, Sunday the 8th, 3:11: twenty-six days. Margot staked out the lounge pull station all night with Theo’s camera and Gold Bond on the handle. She fell asleep at 2:50 for the first time in recorded history. It came from the east stair. Alarm 5, Saturday the 5th, 3:10. Twenty-seven days. Margot said twenty-six. I wasn’t on the lawn. I came up from the water at four. Theo told Priya I was in the shower. Tuesday the 8th, 3:58, three days after: Doug. Asleep. Pillow and all. His hand was on the handle. I was coming in from Burbank. Kevin’s got a chair under the knob.
note:alarm.title: The 3 a.m. alarm

note:assignment.text: Two pages a week, bled on in red. Week two, hers: “That a Broken Statue Is Still Herakles,” with my sentence on page two. Mine: “That God Is the One Who Pays.” She kept it. Then Hale said it out loud: prove the thing you least believe you can prove. Moral luck — mine: “That the Lucky Man Owes Nothing.” Hers: “That There Is Such a Thing as Luck.” Her red on mine: “You don’t believe a word of this. It’s your best paper.” Friendship. Mine: “That a Man and a Woman Can Be Friends.” Hers: “That They Can’t.” She kept mine, and sent it back with *Defense.* in the margin. This week, lying. Mine: “That a Lie Can Be a Kindness.” Hers: “That Every Lie Is a Sin.” We agreed with each other for an hour. Hale asked for a priest.
note:assignment.title: Designated antagonists

note:bigsur.text: Six of us, one van, Highway 1. Father Osei blessed it at seven. South of Lucia a hose clamp backed off and it boiled over. A motel with one heater and a payphone. Kerouac cracked up under Bixby; we drove across it. Gorda gas. A turkey vulture, several times. A condor, once, with a number on its wing. Zebras. Six and oh.
note:bigsur.title: Big Sur

note:cigarette.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven.
note:cigarette.title: The Reliquary

note:driveway.text: The guy at the end of the driveway is my TA.
note:driveway.title: The guy at the end of the driveway

note:fence.text: A gap in the fence behind the Lighthouse; a path along the bluff to the Point. Two people today told me not to go there. Neither would say why.
note:fence.title: The path

note:ferrer.text: A hundred and sixty steps. VIVOS VOCO · MORTUOS PLANGO · FULGURA FRANGO, around the biggest bell. I call the living, I mourn the dead, I break the lightning. One bell is flat. She says it isn’t. Thursday the fifteenth, at five in the morning, we played the Saints on it. Half of Anacapa turned its lights on. Nobody knows who. Margot’s following up for the *Tide*, from a minivan: the police log says one of them was laughing; the bass came in late twice. Nobody confessed. The last day of finals, at noon: ‘Hotel California,’ the flat bell and all. She hummed it.
note:ferrer.title: The Ferrer Tower

note:halloween.text: Theo’s party, on Del Playa. A staircase. Halo or horns. Four hundred Michael Jacksons. Laney was the Pope. Becca was the best saint in Las Olas. Everybody kept calling us American Gothic.
note:halloween.title: Saints & Sinners

note:la_flaca.text: Rafi’s bike, lent till Christmas. Not stolen. Abandoned. (A week’s difference, per his abuela.) Rafi won’t take her back. After Christmas, his abuela says, a bike decides.
note:la_flaca.title: La Flaca

note:laney_advice.text: Laney Price, on romance: a poem, out loud, at a bonfire, about her eyes. It has to rhyme. And then — this is the important part — one knee. Not asking her again. I did the knee. Becca said: Not yet. Halloween: No.
note:laney_advice.title: Laney’s advice

note:ledger.text: Pie: paid. Bus fare: paid, with compliments. Richard Vance’s hundred: Theo’s, for the gas. A new *Brideshead*, cloth, with a ribbon: “Not on the tab.” Postage to Trumbull: $2.38, out of tips. Sully’s: a booth’s worth of nachos and my Cokes, on Meridian Pictures. Theo says Meridian can afford it.
note:ledger.title: The ledger

note:little_way.text: Thérèse of Lisieux. ICS, three dollars off the Driftwood cart, somebody’s highlighter quitting partway. My pencil: *Easy for you.* beside the elevator. *NO.* *She’d have hated Hale.* *Okay, fine.* beside the table of sinners. *Can a man and a woman be friends? Ask L.* beside her two brothers. I gave it to Lena at midnight on her feast. She wouldn’t let me erase a word. She kept it.
note:little_way.title: Story of a Soul

note:magdalena.text: Thursday at Bastille: Julian’s new one. It’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. She watched me hear it. I looked back.
note:magdalena.title: “Magdalena”

note:malibu.text: The bottom half of the pie Post-it, still on the espresso machine in Theo’s hand. Theo says it’s open. I believe him.
note:malibu.title: + 1 Malibu

note:misfit.text: A girl in a window seat had the grandmother down as a con. I said she wanted nothing. She crossed out CON.
note:misfit.title: The Misfit

note:money.text: Spring housing: $340 after aid — the family share that didn’t come. A hold on my registration; my window is Monday at seven and Hale’s seminar fills by five past. Due Friday the 13th, five o’clock. Priya informed me a night desk exists. The hold’s paid. Theo, at the window, in a blazer. The tab: $340.00, plus one pie (peach).
note:money.title: The hold

note:newman.text: The roof is an upside-down boat. The lector reads Deuteronomy like he’s running for Congress. The cantor could make a rock cry.
note:newman.title: St. Brendan’s

note:nonna.text: Asked me about the girl. Laughed. Five minutes later she asked me again, the same words, like it was the first time. Ma says she’s tired. That was the nineteenth of September. Michaelmas she lit one for me and one for Danny. Saturday: ‘E la ragazza?’ Ma told her the girl has a boyfriend. ‘Peccato.’ Then, sharp: ‘E l’altra?’ Purdue Saturday. Dad said ‘Purdue’ and that was the call. Nonna got on the extension and called me Danny. Then she knew me. Then she asked about the crab girl. Sunday the 8th: ‘E la ragazza?’ Which one, I didn’t ask. She didn’t say. Monday she fell on the stairs she’d been keeping off. St. Elizabeth’s: her wrist, six stitches, a monitor for her heart. Called the paramedic handsome. Dad drove her. Home Thanksgiving morning. Cast to the elbow; a monitor on her housedress. Kept both cards — the nun’s and the other one. Made Theo her hands. Sat him in the chair. Says she’ll pray for him, starting that night. Knows it isn’t the nun. Christmas: Mémère’s still lighting her whole name — “Carmela Rinaldi. Tutto.” Asked if Danny’s coming, more than once. Set his place at the Vigil, and Ma left it. Pointed at the girl on the DVD: *l’attrice*. Theo’s cashmere is on her knees.
note:nonna.title: Nonna

note:pelican.text: A girl across the quad won an argument with a parking cop while holding a lamp shaped like a pelican. I didn’t catch her name. I didn’t catch anything. Dad says close your mouth.
note:pelican.title: Pelican girl

note:pie.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. She rated Margot without meeting her: rhubarb — tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit. She rated Becca without meeting her: apple. Honest crust. Nobody loses sleep over an apple. Then she asked what happened to the pecan. A whole pie for a funeral is half price. I work here Tue/Thu/Sat, seven to one. Once a year the kitchen goes dark on a Thursday. Saturday the 10th Gloria met Becca: ‘Apple. Told you, hon.’ She looked at Wes a long time. ‘Peach.’ Everybody likes a peach, she says. Saturday the 12th: boysenberry, for a girl off the TV. Sweet up front, tart after. It stains.
note:pie.title: The Anchor

note:pie_paid.text: Paid Theo one peach pie, Lena’s mother’s crust. Marionberry still 4/10.
note:pie_paid.title: Pie

note:record.text: Two–one after Labor Day; she paid her Sunday. Three–one after moral luck: mine; she said I argued it like it was mine. Now four–one. Friendship: mine, arguing both sides. She said she’d never forgive me. Wednesday she said she forgives me. I’d rather she hadn’t. Unofficial, the laundry room, midnight on her feast, no referee — the Little Way: Thérèse, on points. Unofficial, the Delgado kitchen, a Sunday, no referee — the rich young man: nobody won. She said: He looked at him and loved him. The roux came out perfect. Unofficial, the Brick, four in the morning, no referee — on the heart: nobody won. Official, Hale’s seminar, the day after the Anglicans — on leaving: mine. Five–one. Hale says I argued for leaving like a man who’s never been allowed to. Unofficial, Seacliff Road, Halloween, the hour that happened twice, no referee — on grace: hers. She wants to be asked. Official, Hale’s seminar, All Souls — whether the dead can be wronged: hers. Monica asked to be remembered at the altar, and she was. Five–two. Official, Hale’s table, the night after Fort Hood — go or come away: hers. Leave the light on, she said. Five–three. Unofficial, Kevin’s Odyssey, St. Nicholas Eve, no referee — Nobody: mine, on points. She says I’d have made a terrible Greek.
note:record.title: Duels with Lena

note:roof.text: Fifth floor: EMERGENCY EXIT ONLY · ALARM WILL SOUND, and under it, in Sharpie gone brown: (it won’t). It doesn’t. A popsicle stick in the strike. Tar, gravel, the elevator housing, a parapet to the hip. The Lagoon one way, the hills the other. The last night, three nights before the longest one: the last stop.
note:roof.title: The roof

note:seminar.text: Hale’s seminar. Monday, 1 p.m., Hollis 302. One of the twelve is M. Broussard.
note:seminar.title: PHIL 9H

note:soprano.text: Parish hall, bulletins, lemon bars. “We lost our best soprano last spring.”
note:soprano.title: Mrs. Fitch

note:talk.text: Peter Haddad and Kenzie Rourke, Newman’s it couple, tell their chastity story with a slideshow: Steubenville, 2007; Disneyland; a cousin’s wedding. Margot read them Ephesians. Kenzie answered with verse 25, better than the text deserved. Peter makes the call. Prayerfully.
note:talk.title: Love Is Patient

note:thanksgiving.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing. Becca’s done. It’s me and the Greyhound. Theo’s coming. I asked him at halftime of Michigan; he said yes before I finished. Two seats to Pittsburgh, Wednesday. The Greyhound’s a voucher. Monday Nonna fell. Ma knows about Becca now. Theo and I fly Wednesday — my first time up. Glenwood. Theo in Danny’s bed. Nonna home Thursday. Theo said grace. Trumbull Friday — Theo met Danny. Advent Sunday. Back Sunday night.
note:thanksgiving.title: Thanksgiving

note:the_point.text: A cliff, according to Priya. Nobody goes there after dark. Her rule, not the school’s. Now I know whose rule it is. Went up on Halloween, the second one o’clock, looking for Laney. The old light, dark since 1967. A low stone wall, knee-high on my side and nothing on the other. A white cross: NORA. Somebody’s flowers, two weeks dead, on kitchen string.
note:the_point.title: The Point

note:theo_dawn.text: Came in barefoot at 5:20, sand and wet jeans. ‘Couldn’t sleep.’ There was a girl in our room. Sunday, Sept. 20, 6:10, wet to the shins and hay on his sweater: he says he runs now. Four miles. Barefoot. Sunday, Oct. 11, before light: wet to the shins again. He drives to where he runs. Sunday, Oct. 25, before light, at a motel above Lucia: up the path from the water, wet to the shin, sand on the cashmere. ‘Couldn’t sleep. Went to look at the ocean.’ Sunday, Nov. 1, Halloween’s morning after: asleep on his covers in the dinner jacket at seven, shoes on, sand to the knees, the hems wet. Sunday, Dec. 6, St. Nicholas: at half past five I heard him stand in the open door a long time, and go barefoot. Back at 6:40, wet to the shin and sand above it, with a gas-station coffee and his loafers in his hand.
note:theo_dawn.title: Theo, before light

note:twilight.text: Lena says *Twilight* is the best case for waiting anybody ever sold. We called it a draw. Edward would want us to wait for a ruling.
note:twilight.title: Team Edward

note:wait.text: Wes ended it on All Souls, on the phone. I’m not going to be the rebound. She wants to be asked, and you don’t ask anybody the night her house falls down. When I ask her, she’ll be able to say no. Becca gets an honest ending, in due course, and it’ll be about Becca. I can’t tell Lena what I’m waiting for. Telling her would be asking.
note:wait.title: The wait

note:wall.text: Margot’s board says BOTH, underlined, against her will. Lena made me say it.
note:wall.title: On the Wall

note:whiteboard.text: Margot’s, by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD. Sully’s made the board: liturgical football, idolatry, my outfit. Margot wasn’t even there when I read it. She didn’t need to be. Now the chastity talk is up there too: both of us, voluntarily. Kenzie Rourke got her own line. Margot thinks she might not be an idiot. Category pending. C 6, B 5. The morning after the wake, under the total: TUESDAY — NO SCORE. (BEREAVEMENT.) October 9th, top of the board: LEIF ERIKSON DAY (OBSERVED). Columbus: see attached. Then: FERRER TOWER · THU 5:00 A.M. · “WHEN THE SAINTS GO MARCHING IN.” Suspects: a Catholic; a different Catholic. Laney added the Holy Ghost. Margot wrote it up for the Tide and didn’t name anybody. Halloween: AMERICAN GOTHIC (UNPLANNED). Both. C 7, B 6. Somebody drew a pitchfork. Sunday after St. Nicholas: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS — FLOORS 2–4. SUSPECTS: (THE CATHOLICS). Laney’s TIGER column has given up counting. It says MORE. The last night Lena added a line for Margot to find in January: MARGOT: FEELINGS DETECTED.
note:whiteboard.title: The whiteboard

person:becca.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall.
person:becca.title: Becca Lindell

person:caleb.text: Visalia. Has Hale’s book so full of Post-its it’s molting. Says ‘Selah’ when he means ‘touché.’ Wrote Hale four letters. Hale keeps them. Doesn’t answer them.
person:caleb.title: Caleb (PHIL 9H)

person:carly.text: Mooney ’09, YSU now. Two pews up at Midnight Mass with her mother. Gave me the peace. Asked me to a thing at Ryan’s on New Year’s.
person:carly.title: Carly Benedetto

person:caroline.text: Theo’s mother. Pasadena, she says, and La Cañada now; the hills behind her house are still black. One season of a TV show in the eighties. A Pomeranian named after a painter. Called Becca a Western, and meant it.
person:caroline.title: Caroline Ashby Vance

person:dale.text: Dale Wisniewski. A Lions fan alone at the end of Sully’s bar in a Barry Sanders jersey. Warren, Michigan — not the other one. Tips in quarters. Said the rookie’s going to be good. Lions 38, Browns 37, on the last play. He bought me a root beer: the only man in California who knows what that cost.
person:dale.title: Dale (Sully’s)

person:danny.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140. Fourth letter, All Souls: he knows about hey now. ABOUT TIME, up the margin; he wants to know what she said back. Halloween at Trumbull, a guard in a rubber mask. Ma’s getting Nonno a Mass at St. Brigid’s; he wants me to put Nonno in the book here. He says he’d put his in, but he doesn’t have anybody dead. He has the other kind. I wrote him back: she said hey like she meant it. Thanksgiving weekend: put in for a visit for the rich one himself. Liked him in a minute. Reggie waved. Asked which girl. ‘Who’s Flannery O’Connor?’ Noticed I waited till Theo went to the machines. Told Theo he could quit buying. He went to the prison library about Flannery O’Connor. Ma read it to me off an envelope: she raised peacocks and she was mean and he likes her. Is it still something. The Sunday before Christmas I went with Ma; Pop stayed in the truck — the twenty-seventh, he says. Ma took forever at the machines. He said it for me — I’m in love with Lena — and I didn’t tell him he was wrong. Then the rest: the song, the month, Skye. He said he wasn’t going to tell me which one. He said he believes me, both. Then he asked me one question, and I didn’t have an answer. Then he told Ma I miss the beach. Christmas Eve I brought Theo, in the parka. Theo bought; Danny let him. Theo asked if I’d told him about California. Danny said I miss the beach. Asked Theo who comes to see him. “He does.” Christmas, Gina told him about the boat, and he laughed till they cut him off in the middle of a sentence about Lena.
person:danny.title: Danny Costigan

person:dom.text: Pastor at St. Brigid’s since before I was old enough to serve. Bad left knee, a cough drop through the homily, and he keeps it short on purpose.
person:dom.title: Fr. Dom Bruno

person:doug.text: Doug Pruitt. 420, with Kevin. Bakersfield. Mechanical engineering. A Tauren druid. Says ‘dude’ with five vowels. Tuesday the 8th, 3:58 in the morning, I caught his wrist on the east-stair pull station. He was asleep. The raid boss was in the elevator.
person:doug.title: Doug Pruitt

person:evan.text: Thursday section, Hollis 108. Kierkegaard. Kind to the scared ones, murder on the lazy ones. Smokes American Spirits. Rides a bike. Came back from PERSONAL grayer. Told us we’d left out a driver. Says Kierkegaard was engaged once, gave back the ring, and wrote about her for the rest of his life. Gave back the midterms, then read us Kierkegaard on recollecting the dead — the freest love, because they can’t pay you back. Couldn’t finish the paragraph. After the last section: the man in the white jacket. Was he at Preview Weekend last April? I don’t know. Don’t tell him I asked. I gave him Theo’s name.
person:evan.title: Evan Marsh (TA)

person:frank.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know. Christmas: waited at the bottom of the escalator in Pittsburgh with a thermos and asked about the girl, because Ma told him to. Ginger ale at the bar, in a glass. Stayed in the truck at Trumbull — the twenty-seventh, he says. Drove Theo and me up Christmas Eve and stayed in the truck again. Told Theo Danny ate everything at eleven. Two-eighty-six. Gave Theo the parka without a word. “You’re not company.” Held the 1964 program a long time. On Skye: “Huh.”
person:frank.title: Dad

person:gina.text: My sister. Fifteen, a sophomore at Ursuline. Texts in lowercase like punctuation costs extra. A girl in religion class called her the class expert on visiting the imprisoned. Dad turned the radio back on. Nonna told the altar society I went to confession. Said Danny’s name back to the girl. The girl looked away first. Then laughed with Kelsey anyway. Gina wants the first part on the record. She wanted to know if the nun was real. Now they’re Facebook friends, and Lena signs her wall posts like letters. Gina found the boyfriend in about four minutes. Didn’t tell Nonna. Ashley Vrabel is going to Halloween as a prisoner. Orange jumpsuit. A tribute, she says. Lena read it once and gave me a line for her. Halloween: went as a nun, obviously. Ashley wore the jumpsuit. Gina said it — visit, not dress up as — and Kelsey laughed at Ashley for once. Ashley says she’s dead Monday. Ashley sat next to her in religion and didn’t say anything. Kelsey either. The radio says they’re firing the GM. Dad laughed, Ma says. First time since June. Tuesday she said the thing about Ashley Vrabel’s father in religion. Detention. She thought it would feel good. She heard Dad’s truck hit the can Monday night. Team Edward. Jacob is literally a dog. Monday she found Nonna at the bottom of the stairs, and called the ambulance, and went for Dad. Said sorry to Ashley. Told me in the next text. On the floor in Denver I asked her to look up a girl. She screamed. She’s sworn. ‘Not even the nun?’ Thanksgiving: met me at the door — on TV, in person. Took Danny’s call and said nothing. Printed the dock picture on Ma’s ink. Translated Nonna for Theo, mostly. Checked Facebook for me — Becca took it down. ‘You looked like you were doing a shift.’ Gave Ashley Vrabel the peace at the first candle. Still sworn. Christmas: kept it thirty days. Lifted a hand to Ashley Vrabel at the Orange Julius first, and Ashley lifted one back. Gave me the second season of *Sweetwater*, for research — and Rosie handed it to me in front of everybody. She meant upstairs.
person:gina.title: Gina

person:gloria.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’ The last night: two forks and the pecan, at the counter. ‘That one’s still standing in it, hon.’
person:gloria.title: Gloria (the Anchor)

person:hale.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol.
person:hale.title: Prof. Adrian Hale

person:julian.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight.
person:julian.title: Julian Park-Ellis

person:kevin.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something.
person:kevin.title: Kevin Tran

person:laney.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven.
person:laney.title: Laney Price

person:lena.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else.
person:lena.title: Lena Broussard

person:margot.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research.
person:margot.title: Margot Lindqvist

person:maria.text: Maria Costigan. St. Brigid’s school secretary. Feeds anybody who comes through the door. Cries at grace every year. Took my phone at the table and counted to eleven without looking at it once. Wrote Becca. December 6th, back from Trumbull: the November bill, four hundred and nine texts. Who is it. I told her a girl. Not Lena. Not nice — something. That’s what Dad said about her. Christmas week: took forever at the machines at Trumbull so Danny and I could talk. Stood Becca’s card at the front of the mantel. Brewed the New Orleans coffee Christmas morning. Put unlimited texting on the family plan; it was cheaper than me. Saw the photos. “Is she Catholic, at least?” When Danny laughed on the phone, she looked at me.
person:maria.title: Ma

person:nora.text: The name on the plaque. Priya’s freshman roommate, Delgado 222. From Selma — raisins. Sang soprano; sang the Memorare in the shower. Philosophy. Fell at the Point at the end of April. September 8th would have been her twentieth birthday. Facebook won’t stop suggesting her. Her things are in a box in Priya’s room now. On the inside cover of her journal she promised whoever found it a song. All Souls: Lena wrote her name in the book. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. Julian wrote it too. Her mother wrote Lena for Christmas, care of Newman — the first Christmas; she says she’ll write every one. A picture of Nora on the wall at the Point, laughing. It was Lena’s weekend. The Saturday.
person:nora.title: Nora Calloway

person:odile.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners.
person:odile.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)

person:osei.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back.
person:osei.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei

person:poppy.text: Theo’s sister. Fourteen. He always picks up. Braces and a camera phone. Called me the Catholic.
person:poppy.title: Poppy

person:priya.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning, on her twenty-first birthday. Her mother’s text came in at the dryers. She didn’t answer it in front of me. Alarm Five: the only name on four she couldn’t check was mine. ‘Costigan. You were not on my lawn.’ Sunday at four in the morning she found a card on her door. ‘Unbelievable.’ The last roll, 4:40 a.m., in a headlamp: Costigan — present.
person:priya.title: Priya (RA)

person:rafi.text: Rafi Ochoa. Second floor. Carried my fridge up four flights and was gone before Dad could tip him. Calls everybody boss. Lent me his bike on the wharf at one in the morning like it was nothing, till Christmas. His father’s a detective. He sells weed, and Adderall around midterms. Not bars, he says. Outside the post office he offered me an errand. One ride, Thursday. Two hundred.
person:rafi.title: Rafi Ochoa (204)

person:ray.text: Detective Sergeant, per the badge wallet. Rafi’s father. Gray Crown Vic, a windbreaker, the Vehicle Code by heart. Knows my face from the Anchor counter: Tuesdays, meatloaf, a nod to Rudy. Did the bit: ‘License and registration.’ Asked what was in the bag and took ‘vitamins’ for an answer. Gave me a light out of his trunk. Found property.
person:ray.title: Ray Ochoa (Marisol PD)

person:richard.text: Theo’s father. Learned everybody’s name in one pass but mine; thought I came with the caterer. Calls him Teddy. Stayed six minutes, fourteen seconds. Margot timed it.
person:richard.title: Richard Vance

person:rosie.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab.
person:rosie.title: Rosie

person:rudy.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’ Opened the walk-in on me Tuesday. ‘Mijo. Lettuce.’ Took the lettuce himself. Tuesday, over the Hobart: come hear my mother sing at the Mission, Saturday, five a.m. She came up from Oxnard for the Virgin and sang every verse with her eyes shut.
person:rudy.title: Rudy (the Anchor)

person:skye.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone.
person:skye.title: Skye Callender

person:theo.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule.
person:theo.title: Theo Vance

person:tony.text: Lena’s father. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Twenty-eight years in the same seats. Held the phone up to the kitchen radio for the whole second half while we lost him at every curve on Highway 1. Wes told him there’s a Browns fan out here. Laney had him at hello.
person:tony.title: Tony Broussard

person:wes.text: Lena’s boyfriend. Tulane, civil engineering; the boat at sixteen. Six-two, a chipped front tooth, a Saints cap he’s been bending since 2006. Calls me the Ohio guy. Says she called me a jagoff and that means she likes me; he’s known her since she had a retainer. Drank the Pacific: the jar came back empty. Theo fetched him from the airport alone, in a two-seater, with a sign, and cancelled his motel. Bedbugs, Theo says. He’s on Theo’s new air mattress in our room, three nights. The Corps built the walls wrong; he’s going to build them right. I like him. Saturday night on the beach at Campus Point he waded into the Pacific to the knees. At sixteen he pulled people off roofs for four days in his uncle’s boat. There was one he couldn’t get to — a woman in an attic on Pauger Street; the axe wouldn’t go through. He couldn’t kneel for a year after. Then she came along, he says, and he could. Her Mémère gave him a ring at Easter, for when. He’s going to ask her father after she graduates. He asked me not to say anything to her. He asked me to take care of her. He stopped going to Mass in September. The attic wasn’t over. Mémère asked him about the ring at the tomb on All Saints. He ended it on All Souls, on the phone: she’d marry him anyway, he said, so he couldn’t let her.
person:wes.title: Wes Arceneaux

person:yusuf.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask. The night of the West Point speech: ‘You left the first time. My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.’ His brother Tariq — an IED in Helmand. Alive. Germany. I went after him. We sat on the east stairs. Back for finals the night before Oslo. Tariq’s learning stairs. He’d like the speech to be right. Tariq home the twenty-third. Fourteen stairs; he’s done eleven. A fifth rail.
person:yusuf.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)

keys.text: You shook your father’s hand goodbye.
Lena took the cigarette out of your mouth.
You walked Lena and Laney home.
You gave Fr. Osei a straight answer about the scar, and he didn’t push.
At Mass you prayed for the girl three pews up.
You followed Lena out of the Anchor.
You let Lena know you were on the stairs.
You hit Reply All.
You told Hale he’d inherited his atheism too.
You took Theo’s money as a loan, payable in pie.
You told your father you’d taken a job washing dishes.
You played chess with Fr. Osei instead of going to confession.
You told Lena you’d been worried she had bad taste.
You wrote on Lena’s wall at two in the morning.
You walked Laney to Pi Lam with Lena.
You told Theo you couldn’t afford Los Angeles.
You told Theo God is the one who pays.
You told Margot a nun gave you the scar.
You told Nonna you played chess with the priest instead of going to confession.
You spent Sunday afternoon at the Getty Villa with Lena.
You gave Richard Vance’s hundred to Theo for the gas.
You told Lena your father’s been laid off since June.
You told Theo where your brother is.
You gave Lena’s reliquary its second relic.
You asked Rudy who came to see him inside.
You lit Priya’s candle for Nora.
You told the lounge the congressman had no right to call that man a liar.
You broke the fast with Yusuf.
You went after Lena in the middle of the song.
Lena smoked half of your cigarette, then put it in the tin.
You told Lena your brother is in prison.
You called her Magdalena, and she let you.
You went to confession, like Nonna said.
You said the unlucky driver owes everything — that nobody gets to take it for him.
You told Lena the argument was about your brother.
You showed Lena your sister’s text.
You gave Gina the nun’s advice: say his name.
You told Theo that Lena knows about Danny.
You spent Pref Night on the floor of 217 with Laney and Lena.
You told Laney they’d be lucky to have her.
Lena said hello to your brother.
You texted Lena back: 61.
You told Hale your brother is in prison.
You told Becca a Franciscan gave you the scar in a pickup game.
Becca asked if the cleanup was a date. You said it was both.
When Nonna asked about the girl a second time, you answered her like it was the first.
At the creek mouth you offered Lena your arm, and she took it.
Lena asked if the cleanup was a date. You said Becca’s lovely and you don’t know what you’re doing.
When Lena said she’d decided not to notice, you told her she doesn’t have to be fine with you.
You read Lena your brother’s letter: ‘Tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. I got it.’
You told Lena that Nonna asked you the same question twice.
At the elevator you said, “Goodnight, Magdalena.” Twice now.
You let Gloria pick the funeral pie. She picked pecan.
On the roof Lena took a clove out of your mouth. Reliquary No. 4 — by dispensation.
Mid-argument on the roof, you said Lena’s name to stop her.
You gave Margot your flannel and didn’t say anything.
On the roof at dawn Lena said she hadn’t finished a sentence. You told her you’d noticed.
When Lena told you Wes is coming for Columbus Day, you said okay.
In Hale’s seminar you said C.S. Lewis had already married his friend when he wrote the friendship chapter.
Hale gave you a pocket Housman for your brother. If Danny asks who sent it: a man who doesn’t sleep.
Thursday you went to the *Tide* office when Margot said she needed a Catholic.
On the bleachers Becca asked if you ever think it might not be true. You said not whether it’s true: whether you’re any good at it, at two in the morning.
Your mother asked about the veil girl. You told her she has a boyfriend.
Sunday you watched the Saints with Lena at Sully’s.
At midnight on her feast you gave Lena a secondhand *Story of a Soul*. “Happy feast day, Magdalena Thérèse.”
At midnight on her feast Lena read you Thérèse’s ‘empty hands.’ You asked her to read it again.
At Lupe’s, Lena found your margin — *Ask L.* You told her you wanted to know if it counts: a man and a woman, by letters.
At Shipwreck Cove Lena taught you the Cajun waltz to “Jolie Blonde.”
At the waterline Lena asked if you knew what you were doing. You said Becca’s nice. She laughed. You told her she looked relieved. She said she wasn’t.
At four in the morning you walked Lena up the stairs. At the second floor she sent you to bed.
You asked Becca out for Friday: the elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset. You asked, and you’re paying.
Friday night on the Portolá steps, you kissed Becca.
At the Blessing of the Animals you and Lena managed about five minutes of being careful. Then you set her off again, in front of Becca.
Sunday you watched the Saints go four and oh with Lena at Sully’s.
At dawn in the Marine Lab, Becca showed you how an anemone holds on.
On the curb you finally gave Lena your brother’s message. “Hey back,” she said. “I said it myself.”
In the Anacapa lot you said “Who dat” to Wes Arceneaux. He picked you up off the asphalt.
At the bonfire Becca asked where you learned the waltz. You told her: Lena.
At the bonfire you read Becca a poem about her freckles and finished it on one knee. “Not yet, Jack Costigan.”
At the last house on Seacliff, Lena wouldn’t go on to the Point. You walked her back.
On the beach at two in the morning you told Wes your brother’s in prison.
On the beach Wes showed you a picture of a ring and asked you to take care of her. You drank instead of answering. He took it for a yes.
Sunday you went to the 9:30 with Becca, Lena and Wes.
At the stove, arguing the rich young man, you told Lena you’re both the sad one, some days.
In the lot Monday Wes shook your hand instead of hugging you. You said “Who dat.” He said it back.
In the flooded basement you helped Priya carry Nora’s box upstairs. She wouldn’t open the journal past the first page.
In the stairwell at four in the morning you told Lena the truth about the beach: you drank, and Wes took it for a yes.
At five in the morning Lena played the Saints on the Ferrer Tower, and you took the low notes.
When the police came, you ran for the library with her, laughing.
At seven the bells woke her on your shoulder. You said her name.
Thursday you watched the balloon in the Fishbowl. Lena watched the news crawl under it.
On the Delgado steps at one in the morning, Laney told you about Kaylee.
After *Where the Wild Things Are*, Becca said you look at her like homework. She said she’ll wait.
You asked Becca to come to Big Sur. She couldn’t: Thomas needs her.
Two–two in the van, you voted for Vespers with the monks.
At the payphone the quarters ran out. “Kevin’s got another roll.” “I know he does.”
On the motel porch under the Milky Way you lit a Red. Lena came out and took it: No. 6.
On the porch at three in the morning Lena asked what you decided. “Not to be the one who wrecks anything.” “Me neither.”
On the hill you showed Lena Gina’s text about Ashley Vrabel. Lena gave you a line for her.
When Porter picked it off, Lena grabbed you. You yelled WHO DAT at her father.
You handed in your homework six days early: St. Isidore and St. Maria — her first one.
Becca asked who Lena was being. You told her: a Catholic writer from Georgia.
When the party chanted American Gothic, you brought Becca up the stairs yourself. “I’m with Maria.”
On the widow’s walk Lena asked if this was the occasion. Reliquary No. 7.
At the Point you found Theo at the wall. You stayed back on the path and talked.
Theo asked you to tell them he was looking for Laney. You asked him to come to Lupe’s instead.
Lena asked if anybody was up there. You said just the cross.
In the last minute of the extra hour, you took off the hat. Lena put it back on your head.
Laney asked who your candle at the monks was for. You said your brother.
On All Souls you wrote your grandfather’s name in the Book of the Dead, and started another line, and left it.
At half past four on the stairs she asked you for one. Reliquary No. 8.
At dawn on the stairs you decided not to be the rebound. She wants to be asked — not the night her house fell.
At dawn she asked what you were going to do. “Whatever you need.”
For Theo’s nineteenth you gave him your own copy of *The Moviegoer*, margins and all.
Tuesday you wrote 7–0 on the Odyssey’s glass in her polish.
At Theo’s birthday Caroline asked how long you and Lena had been together. “We’re not. Becca’s with me.”
When Lena left Theo’s birthday early, Laney kicked you under the table, and you went.
At the Anchor you told Gloria you won’t be the next guy at the door.
On the Portolá steps Becca asked if she could tell her mom you’re her boyfriend. You said yes, and meant to mean it.
At Hale’s table you told Lena to leave the light on.
When the dinner turned, you found Lena on Hale’s deck with his dog.
Walking down from Hale’s cliff, Lena told you she’s known about your postcard since the porch — and then about the house she’d already furnished in her head.
The Saturday after Hale’s dinner you took Lena to the harbor fish market, and she bought a rockfish for the night shift.
Saturday at 3:30 you went to confession after Lena.
Walking home at one in the morning, Lena said she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. You took her to Lupe’s.
At Sully’s you told Becca you’re going to ask Lena to Youngstown for Thanksgiving.
On the phone you told your mother a friend from school might come for Thanksgiving. Lena.
On the courtyard wall Lena told you Julian asked her to Bastille on Thursday. You said you’d be there.
At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You prayed the Sorrowful Mysteries with her until the truck pulled in.
Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You took her hand and told her to keep Daisy.
On the bench above Campus Point you told Lena about your father’s night in the Lordstown lot.
You let Theo pay the hold. It’s on the tab.
Under the eucalyptus Lena mentioned that Julian asked her to dinner. You asked if she was happy. She said yes.
Gina asked if the nun was coming for Thanksgiving. You wrote back: no. just me.
In Eli’s truck you told Becca you’re not right for her.
The night you ended it you went to confession. Your penance: pray for Becca by name, every day, until Advent.
Lena came up in her socks to ask if you were okay. You told her why: you couldn’t take Becca home.
In the basement, about Edward leaving Bella for her own good, you told Lena: “He should have asked her.”
On the piano bench, when Lena’s hand found the same key, you didn’t move yours.
Friday Lena signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed with a cold. You signed it too.
At Wyatt Halloran’s party you crossed the room yourself.
In the window seat, over O’Connor, you told her what the grandmother wanted at the end: nothing. That’s the point.
In the water at Ellery Beach she asked about the scar. You told her a jealous husband in Erie, Pennsylvania.
Soaking wet on the sand at Ellery Beach, she said, “I’d like to kiss you now.” You kissed her before she finished.
On the sand at Ellery Beach she was the one who stopped.
At six in the morning Theo asked where you went. You said you argued about a book till it got light.
At halftime of Ohio State–Michigan you asked Theo home to Youngstown for Thanksgiving. He said yes before you finished.
Your first text to Skye was a correction: *the grandmother still gets the last word. —jack (the guy who was right).*
On the courtyard wall you told Lena that Theo dragged you to a party in Montecito. You didn’t tell her the rest.
The day Nonna fell, you told your mother Becca wasn’t coming at Christmas. ‘It wasn’t right.’
In the margin of Lena’s paper you wrote: *Persuasive. Unfortunately also correct.*
At the Starlite she cast you as O’Connor’s Bible salesman, and you committed.
At the Starlite Skye asked what believing is like. You said: like being known, and not getting thrown out.
At the Starlite she asked you to miss her a reasonable amount. You said you’d keep a ledger.
In the Anacapa lot you didn’t ask. You kissed her.
Against the Saab she was the one who stopped.
Before dawn Theo asked what you’d been doing. ‘I run now.’
On the floor in Denver you asked Gina to be your Facebook detective.
From the floor in Denver you texted Skye that you’d explained GM to a girl who’s on TV Thursdays at nine.
At the door Gina held out a printout of Skye. You gave her Skye’s message instead: Cassidy says be nice.
At the table your mother held out her hand for the phone. You kissed it first, then gave it to her.
Before Trumbull you texted Skye the truth: your brother’s in prison.
When Danny told Theo he could quit buying, you rescued him with a joke.
Theo asked if Danny ever says he’s sorry. You told him what Danny says: he doesn’t wish. He decides.
At two in the morning she asked what you think about, and you told her — all of it, in the basement, with your grandmother asleep overhead.
On the porch she asked for your family. You did Gina finding out.
On the porch she asked if the TV part matters. You said no — she had the grandmother backwards, and that’s the part you know.
At breakfast Theo’s phone said you and Skye are friends now. You talked about the ricotta.
At the first candle you prayed for Skye by name, the first time.
Nonna asked who’s writing you. You told her: a girl. An actress.
At Sully’s you left an eleven-and-oh game at the two-minute warning. “I’ve seen how it ends.”
When Yusuf’s phone lit up FREMONT — HOME during the speech, you went after him.
At five in the morning she sent you a picture from a makeup chair. You told her she looked tired, and good.
After section Evan asked about the man in the white jacket. You gave him a name: Theo Vance.
Up the coast at one in the morning she asked you to LA. You said you wanted to, and that you work Saturdays.
In a turnout where the coast turns, you let her lead.
Saturday you went into the box and told Fr. Osei about a girl.
At the Anchor, with Lena at the counter, you put your phone on silent and kept it in your pocket.
In the Walgreens Lena asked where you go. You said you’d tell her sometime. Not yet.
In Kevin’s Odyssey Lena gave you Homer. You said Penelope waited twenty years for a man who lied his way home.
In the laundry room Lena stepped back first. You told her you don’t want to be the one either — that that’s the whole trouble.
Sunday morning, with her second picture still in your phone, you told her you hadn’t stopped seeing it.
Your mother counted four hundred and nine texts on the November bill and asked who. You told her: a girl.
After the nine o’clock Julian asked you to stay to the end of his new song on Thursday. You said you would.
In Burbank, in the first storm of the winter, you stood under a rain tower in your blazer so they could light her face.
At four in the morning you caught Doug Pruitt asleep at the pull station. You woke Kevin.
On the Immaculate Conception you got up on three hours’ sleep for the 12:10.
Tuesday night, in the Anchor’s walk-in, you opened her third picture. You told her you can’t stop looking at it.
At the Brick you chose the argument of Lena’s you’ll defend for Hale: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason.
At Bastille Julian sang a song called “Magdalena.” Lena watched you hear it, and you looked back.
On her bed on Del Playa you put your hand over hers on the buckle and said no.
At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and gave her C. S. Lewis on hating what a man does and still loving the man — the way you already love yourself.
At four in the morning you told her it’s a no right now — not always, just now. She said she can work with that. You told her it isn’t her you don’t trust.
At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You asked her to meet you somewhere in daylight.
At ten past six Theo asked why you look like you’ve been through a warzone. You told him you were out.
Lena’s text from the night of the song was still waiting at noon. You didn’t answer it.
At the Newman party Gus asked if anybody plays. You know Lena does. You said nothing.
Friday night she took your “right now” apart, and nearly won. You told her you want her, and it’s still no.
To the letter: she stopped where you said no, and went no further. You let everything else run, and the line held.
Under the roses at five in the morning Lena said you were up early. You told her you couldn’t sleep. She said Theo told her you were at the library, at half past twelve.
On Saturday you went into the box and told Father Osei about a week of her, and the door you left open.
Father Osei asked if you can say no every night to a woman who heard you the first time. You told him not by yourself — that’s why you were in there.
Saturday, in the east stairwell, you opened her fourth picture — your own shirt — and told her you want it back, and her in it.
At 11:52 Lena texted: Pie? You didn’t answer.
At one in the morning on the wharf she said she’ll ask every day. Then she asked you home, to sleep. You went.
At ten to ten on Gaudete Sunday she offered you breakfast at the Starlite. You went, and missed the Saints.
On the night of the Geminids Lena called from the roof while you were on the lawn with Skye on the phone. You let it ring out.
Tuesday, in the Saab at the turnout, she asked. You let her get as far as the zipper. Then you said no.
At Hale’s oral he asked if you believe her argument. You said you believe it because you watched her live it.
Wednesday at eight you went into the box.
At one in the morning on the bluff, Skye said not before Christmas — in January, officially, a whole thing. You told her yes, you want that.
On the bluff she didn’t ask, and you were the one who went too far. You took one more minute. Then you said no.
Theo held up the tab. You let him tear it up.
On the Lighthouse porch Lena named the month — the texts, Sully’s, the staying away. You told her you were sorry, and not why.
At the Point Lena showed you a photograph her letter came with. You reached for your cigarettes, and she took one for the tin.
On the roof, three nights before the longest night, you started to say it, and stopped yourself.
In Trumbull’s visiting room you told Danny about the girl in California, and he finished the sentence for you: you’re in love with Lena.
Danny didn’t tell you which one. He asked you one thing — which of them you can tell the truth to — and you asked him how he does it, in there.
The Monday night after the solstice Lena called at ten to one to argue about Pius XII. When she started to let you go, you asked her not to hang up yet.
At twenty to three in the morning Skye told you she and Theo have known each other since they were eleven, and that he knows about you two. You asked if he did the bow.
On Christmas Eve morning you went to confession at St. Brigid’s.
On Christmas Eve Lena held her phone up to a bonfire on the levee. You told her you wished you were standing next to her.
Christmas Eve, behind the bathroom’s hook-and-eye, you opened the picture Skye sent and answered it.
In Danny’s room at three on Christmas morning Theo said Merry Christmas from the dark, and you called him Ted.
Christmas morning, with Gina’s DVD in your hands, your mother asked if that was the girl. You told her: that’s her, her name’s Skye.
Christmas night, from the back steps on Dupre Street, Lena told you her mother worked at Memorial. You asked if she wanted to tell you.
